import bt,numpy as np
n=bt.signals();R=bt.train_returns().astype(float)
sh=R.mean(0)/R.std(0)*np.sqrt(252)
fam=np.array([s.split('_')[0] for s in n])
for f in set(fam): print(f,(fam==f).sum(),sh[fam==f].mean().round(2),(sh[fam==f]>0).mean().round(2))
def ev(w): return bt.backtest(w)
# candidates
allw={s:1 for s in n}
print('all',ev(allw))
for f in ['tsmom','ma','hold']:
    print(f,ev({s:1 for s,g in zip(n,fam) if g==f}))
# equal-risk, sign by train sharpe across tsmom+ma
vol=R.std(0)
w={s:(1/v)*1 for s,v,g in zip(n,vol,fam) if g!='hold'}
print('tsmom+ma invvol',ev(w))
# half-train sharpe consistency
h=len(R)//2
s1=R[:h].mean(0)/R[:h].std(0);s2=R[h:].mean(0)/R[h:].std(0)
ok=(s1>0)&(s2>0)&(fam!='hold')
print(ok.sum(),ev({s:1/v for s,v,o in zip(n,vol,ok) if o}))
E

I submitted an inverse-volatility-weighted portfolio of the 71 tsmom and ma signals that earned a positive return in both halves of the 1970-1999 training period. Its Sharpe was about 1.0 in training and 0.22 in validation, and I expect it to do worse on 2013 onward than the training figure suggests.

I found no family-level or lookback-level edge, and the more aggressively I picked the best training signals, the worse they did in validation (top 20 and top 50 by training Sharpe both came out slightly negative). I chose this broader, more diversified version because it was the only selection that stayed positive in validation.
